cost equals one-way turnover x 2 x bps/1e4 in NAV units

wrong_answers.label: charge cost on one-way turnover only
wrong_answers.reason: Both the buy and the matching sell pay the cost; one-way turnover must be doubled to get traded notional.

wrong_answers.label: break-even ignoring the management fee
wrong_answers.reason: The fee is paid regardless, so it reduces the room available for trading costs.

limitations: Linear cost model; impact actually grows with trade size relative to liquidity.

title: Factor regression: alpha, residual risk and information ratio
mechanism: OLS decomposition of strategy returns into factor exposure and residual alpha with correct alpha standard error
decision_relevance: Whether a strategy adds value beyond a cheap factor exposure
prompt: Monthly excess returns (decimal) of a strategy r_t and a single factor f_t are given for 36 months. Fit r_t = alpha + beta f_t + e_t by OLS. Report (1) beta, (2) alpha in percent per month, (3) the t-statistic of alpha using the homoskedastic OLS standard error SE(alpha)=s_e*sqrt(1/T + fbar^2/Sxx) with s_e the residual standard deviation using T-2 degrees of freedom, and (4) the annualised information ratio alpha/s_e*sqrt(12).
solution: Sxy/Sxx gives beta = 0.5284; alpha = rbar - beta fbar = 0.3750% per month. Residual sd s_e = 1.1899%/month; SE(alpha) = 0.1984% so t = 1.891. IR = 0.00375/0.01190 x sqrt(12) = 1.092. R^2 = 0.568.

checks.name: OLS residuals sum to zero
OLS residuals are orthogonal to the factor
R^2 from SSR/SST equals the squared sample correlation

wrong_answers.label: alpha as simple mean difference r - f (assumes beta=1)
wrong_answers.reason: Only valid if beta equals one; the fitted beta is about 0.528, so subtracting the full factor mean gives a different intercept.

wrong_answers.label: information ratio using total strategy volatility
wrong_answers.reason: The IR scales alpha by the residual (idiosyncratic) risk, not the total risk that includes factor exposure.

limitations: Homoskedastic SE; single factor; synthetic series built from a known linear relation plus noise.

title: HAC t-statistic and autocorrelation-adjusted annual volatility
mechanism: Newey-West Bartlett-weighted long-run variance for the mean and the exact variance of 12-month sums
decision_relevance: Whether positive autocorrelation makes a monthly mean return look more significant and less volatile than it is
prompt: A strategy has T=120 monthly returns, sample mean 0.60% and sample standard deviation 2.50%. Autocorrelations are rho1=0.25, rho2=0.10, rho3=0.05 and zero beyond lag 3. Treat gamma_0 as sd^2 and gamma_k as sd^2 rho_k, with no finite-sample divisor correction. Report (1) the naive t-statistic of the mean (sd/sqrt(T) standard error), (2) the Newey-West t-statistic using the Bartlett kernel with lag length L=3 (weights 1-k/(L+1)), (3) the long-run variance factor, i.e. the ratio of the HAC variance of the mean to the naive variance, and (4) the annual volatility in percent computed from the exact variance of a sum of 12 consecutive monthly returns using the given autocorrelations (no kernel truncation).

outputs.name: long_run_variance_factor
outputs.description: HAC variance / naive variance of the mean

solution: Bartlett weights 0.75, 0.5, 0.25 give factor 1+2(0.1875+0.05+0.0125) = 1.5000. SE_naive = 0.2282%, t_naive = 2.629; SE_HAC = SE_naive x sqrt(1.500) so t_HAC = 2.147. Annual variance of a 12-month sum = sd^2[12 + 2 sum_k (12-k) rho_k] = sd^2 x 20.400; vol = 11.292% versus sqrt(12) scaling 8.660%.

checks.name: zero autocorrelation limiting case gives factor exactly 1
Bartlett-weighted factor is below the untruncated sum 1+2*sum(rho)
12-month variance factor equals direct double sum of the autocovariance matrix

wrong_answers.label: unweighted sum of autocorrelations (no Bartlett kernel)
wrong_answers.reason: Newey-West with the Bartlett kernel down-weights higher lags to guarantee a positive estimate; using raw sums gives a different factor.

wrong_answers.label: sqrt(12) annualisation of volatility
wrong_answers.reason: sqrt(time) scaling assumes uncorrelated returns; positive autocorrelation raises multi-period variance.

wrong_answers.label: divide instead of multiply the variance by the factor
wrong_answers.reason: Positive autocorrelation lowers the effective sample size and must inflate the standard error.

limitations: Autocorrelations are treated as known; in practice they are estimated with error and the lag choice matters.

title: Expected maximum Sharpe under the null and family-wise p-values
mechanism: Extreme-value approximation of the best-of-N null Sharpe and Sidak/Bonferroni family-wise correction
decision_relevance: Whether the best of 40 backtests is evidence of skill or just selection
prompt: A researcher runs N=40 independent strategy variants whose true Sharpe ratios are all zero. Across the trials the estimated annual Sharpe ratios have standard deviation 0.30. Use the approximation E[max of N standard normals] ~ (1-g) Z(1-1/N) + g Z(1-1/(N e)) with g the Euler-Mascheroni constant 0.5772 and Z the standard normal quantile. The best variant has t-statistic 2.40 against zero. Report (1) the expected maximum annual Sharpe under the null, (2) the two-sided single-test p-value of the best variant (normal approximation), (3) the Sidak family-wise p-value 1-(1-p)^N, and (4) whether the best variant is significant at the 5% family-wise level using the Sidak p-value.

outputs.name: expected_max_sharpe
outputs.description: expected best Sharpe under the null

solution: Z(1-1/40) = 1.9600, Z(1-1/(40e)) = 2.3576; E[max] = 0.30 x 2.1895 = 0.6568. Single p = 2(1-Phi(2.4)) = 0.0164. Sidak p = 1-(1-0.0164)^40 = 0.4838 (Bonferroni 0.6558); not significant family-wise. The expected best null Sharpe 0.66 illustrates selection bias; the observed best variant does not pass the stated family-wise 5% test.

checks.name: extreme-value approximation vs numerical integration of E[max of N normals]
Sidak p-value never exceeds Bonferroni

wrong_answers.label: ignore multiplicity and use the single-test p-value
wrong_answers.reason: With 40 trials the chance that at least one reaches |t|>2.4 under the null is about 48%.

wrong_answers.label: use only the Z(1-1/N) term for the expected maximum
wrong_answers.reason: The 1-1/N quantile understates the expected maximum; the Euler-Mascheroni term corrects it.

limitations: Trials treated as independent; correlated variants reduce the effective number of trials.

title: Bayesian shrinkage of a noisy return forecast
mechanism: Normal-normal conjugate update of an expected-return forecast toward a zero prior
decision_relevance: How much of a raw analyst signal should be believed before sizing a position
prompt: A quantitative signal produces a raw forecast of next month excess return for a stock of +2.00% (monthly, percent). Prior to seeing the signal, the true expected monthly excess return is believed to be normally distributed with mean 0 and standard deviation 0.50%. The forecast equals the true expected return plus independent normal noise with standard deviation 1.50%. Report (1) the shrinkage factor (posterior mean divided by raw forecast), (2) the posterior mean in % per month, (3) the posterior standard deviation of the true expected return in % per month, and (4) the posterior probability that the true expected return is positive.
solution: k = tau^2/(tau^2+sigma^2) = 0.25/2.5 = 0.100; posterior mean = 0.200%; posterior variance = tau^2 sigma^2/(tau^2+sigma^2) = 0.2250 so sd = 0.4743%. P(mu>0) = Phi(0.200/0.4743) = 0.6634. The posterior mean is 90% smaller than the raw forecast. A position size cannot be determined without a risk model and sizing objective.

checks.name: precision-weighted average reproduces the posterior mean
posterior variance equals 1/(prior precision + noise precision)
posterior sd is below both the prior sd and the noise sd

wrong_answers.label: take the raw forecast at face value
wrong_answers.reason: The forecast noise variance is nine times the prior variance; most of the raw number is noise.

wrong_answers.label: reverse the weights (shrink by sigma^2/(tau^2+sigma^2))
wrong_answers.reason: The weight on the data is the prior variance share, not the noise variance share.

wrong_answers.label: posterior sd equals the forecast noise sd
wrong_answers.reason: Combining prior and data increases precision; the posterior sd must be below both.

limitations: Gaussian conjugate model; non-normal signals or time-varying noise need a different update.

title: AR(1) spread: half-life, stationary dispersion and expected path
family: time-series state estimation and mean reversion
mechanism: Mapping a discrete AR(1) regression of spread changes into half-life, long-run mean and stationary variance
decision_relevance: Whether a spread deviation is large relative to its equilibrium dispersion and how fast it should revert
prompt: A daily pairs spread s_t (in spread points) has been fitted with the regression s_{t+1} - s_t = a + b s_t + e_t, giving a=0.60, b=-0.08 and residual standard deviation 0.90 points (e_t iid, mean zero). Today the spread is 10.20. Report (1) the half-life of a deviation in trading days (continuous, not rounded), (2) the long-run mean, (3) the stationary standard deviation of the spread, (4) the current z-score (deviation from the long-run mean divided by the stationary sd), and (5) the expected spread five trading days from now.

outputs.name: z_score
outputs.description: current deviation in stationary sd units

solution: phi = 1+b = 0.92, mu = -a/b = 7.50. Half-life = ln 0.5/ln 0.92 = 8.313 days. Stationary variance = 0.81/(1-0.92^2) so sd = 2.2964. z = (10.2-7.50)/2.2964 = 1.176. E[s_5] = mu + phi^5 (s-mu) = 9.2795. The spread is only 1.18 sd rich, a modest signal given the roughly eight-day half-life.

checks.name: after one half-life the expected deviation is exactly halved
stationary variance as fixed point of V = phi^2 V + sigma^2 by iteration

wrong_answers.label: continuous-time half-life ln2/|b|
wrong_answers.reason: For a discrete AR(1) the decay factor is phi=1+b, and ln(0.5)/ln(phi) differs from ln2/|b| by a third of a day here.

wrong_answers.label: z-score using the residual sd
wrong_answers.reason: The residual sd is the one-step innovation; the unconditional dispersion is larger by 1/sqrt(1-phi^2).

limitations: Assumes the fitted AR(1) is stationary and parameters are known without estimation error.

title: Purged and embargoed cross-validation fold sizes
mechanism: Counting training labels whose forward-looking windows overlap a contiguous test fold, with an embargo
decision_relevance: How much training data must be dropped to keep a backtest CV estimate honest
prompt: A supervised strategy model is trained on N=1000 consecutive daily observations indexed 0..999. The label of observation i is the return from the close of day i to the close of day i+h with h=10, so its label window spans days i to i+10 inclusive. A 5-fold contiguous split is used (folds of 200 observations). Consider the test fold with indices 400..599. Purging removes any training observation whose label window overlaps the union of the test label windows (days 400 to 609). An embargo further removes the 5 training observations immediately after the last purged index following the test block. Report (1) the number of training observations that remain, (2) the number purged before the test block, (3) the number removed after the test block (purge plus embargo), and (4) the fraction of the naive 800 training observations whose labels overlap the test label span if no purge is applied.

outputs.name: n_train
outputs.description: training observations after purge and embargo

outputs.name: leak_fraction_unpurged
outputs.description: overlapping share of the naive 800 training observations

solution: Before the test block, i+10 >= 400 for i in 390..399: 10 purged. After it, i <= 609 for i in 600..609: 10 purged, plus embargo 610..614: 5. Training = 1000-200-10-10-5 = 775. Without purging 20/800 = 0.0250 of training labels share inclusive label windows with the test span. The stated conservative purge policy counts even a shared boundary date.

checks.name: direct enumeration over all indices with the overlap rule reproduces n_train
purged counts on each side equal the horizon h

wrong_answers.label: purge only after the test block (forgetting pre-test labels look forward into it)
wrong_answers.reason: Observations 390..399 have labels that end inside the test window; they must be purged too.

wrong_answers.label: embargo without purge
wrong_answers.reason: An embargo alone leaves the 20 overlapping labels in the training set.

limitations: Single fold illustrated; other folds (first/last) have one-sided purges.

title: Signal alignment: look-ahead versus correctly lagged backtest
mechanism: Aligning a close-based signal with the return it can actually earn, exposing same-bar look-ahead
decision_relevance: Whether a backtest is inflated by using a signal computed from the bar it is traded on
prompt: Twelve daily closes are given (days 0..11). A 3-day momentum signal on day t is +1 if close_t > close_{t-3}, -1 if lower, 0 if equal (defined for t>=3). A correctly implemented backtest trades at the close of day t and holds the position over the return from close_t to close_{t+1}, for t = 3..10 (eight holding periods). A look-ahead implementation instead applies the signal of day t to the return from close_{t-1} to close_t, for the same returns ending on days 4..11. For this idealised timing exercise, execution at the exact signal-day close is permitted with no latency or slippage. Returns are simple and compounded multiplicatively, no costs. Report (1) the cumulative return of the correct backtest in percent, (2) the cumulative return of the look-ahead backtest in percent, and (3) their difference in percentage points.

outputs.name: correct_cum_return_pct
outputs.description: compounded return, signal lagged one bar

solution: Correct: position at t uses sign(close_t - close_(t-3)) and earns close_t->close_(t+1); compounding eight periods gives -2.758%. Look-ahead: the signal on day t already contains close_t, the end of the return it is applied to, giving 1.113%. Inflation 3.871 points. Adding an extra day of delay (two-bar lag) would give 1.131%, showing the cost of latency.

checks.name: look-ahead run reproduced by direct per-day enumeration on raw closes
look-ahead run beats the correct run in this sample

wrong_answers.label: report the look-ahead result as the strategy return
wrong_answers.reason: A signal using close_t cannot be traded before close_t; the return it is applied to must start at close_t.

wrong_answers.label: lag the signal by two bars (over-conservative) and call it correct
wrong_answers.reason: The stated execution is at the close of the signal day; a second day of delay understates the achievable return.

limitations: Tiny sample for illustration; sign conventions for zero-change days are stated.

title: Square-root market impact: cost, size elasticity and maximum order
mechanism: Square-root impact law in participation of ADV, dollar-cost elasticity and inverting for a cost budget
decision_relevance: How large an order can be before impact breaches a cost budget, and how cost scales with size
prompt: An order to buy Q=250,000 shares of a stock priced at $40.00 is executed over one day. Average daily volume is 2,000,000 shares and daily volatility is 2.2%. Market impact per share (as a fraction of price) follows the square-root law Y * sigma_daily * sqrt(Q/ADV) with Y=0.8. In addition, each share pays a half-spread of 3 bps. Report (1) the impact cost in bps of price, (2) the total execution cost in dollars (impact plus half-spread on all shares), (3) the elasticity of the total impact dollar cost with respect to order size (d ln cost / d ln Q), and (4) the maximum order size in shares for which impact alone stays at or below 40 bps. Treat order size as continuous for this budget calculation.
solution: Participation Q/ADV = 0.125, sqrt = 0.3536; impact = 0.8 x 0.022 x 0.3536 = 62.23 bps; total per share 65.23 bps; dollars = 250000 x 40 x 65.23/1e4 = $65,225. Dollar impact ~ Q^1.5 so elasticity = 1.50. Budget 40 bps: Q_max = ADV (0.004/(Y sigma))^2 = 103,306 shares.

checks.name: impact recomputed at q_max equals the 40 bps budget
elasticity from doubling matches analytic 1.5 of the square-root law
total cost reconciles as shares x price x (impact+spread)/1e4

wrong_answers.label: linear impact scaling when inverting the budget
wrong_answers.reason: Under the square-root law impact per share grows with sqrt(Q), so the budget-compliant size is proportional to the square of the ratio.

wrong_answers.label: use annualised volatility in the daily impact formula
wrong_answers.reason: The square-root law is calibrated with volatility over the execution horizon (one day), not annual.

wrong_answers.label: omit the half-spread
wrong_answers.reason: Crossing the spread is a real cost on every share in addition to impact.

limitations: Single-day execution; Y is a stylised constant and impact decay is ignored.

title: Adverse-selection spread with sequential Bayesian quote updating
mechanism: Glosten-Milgrom zero-profit quotes as conditional expectations, updated trade by trade
decision_relevance: How a market maker must widen and skew quotes against informed order flow
prompt: A risk-neutral competitive market maker quotes a stock whose end-of-day value is either 102 or 98, each with prior probability 0.5. Each arriving trader is informed with probability 0.30 (knows the value and buys if 102, sells if 98) and otherwise uninformed (buys or sells with probability 0.5 each). Trader types and uninformed directions are independent across arrivals conditional on the fixed end-of-day value. Each trade is one unit. Quotes are set so that the market maker breaks even in expectation conditional on the trade direction (ask = E[V | buy], bid = E[V | sell]). Report (1) the initial ask, (2) the initial bid, (3) the initial spread, and (4) the ask quoted after two consecutive buys have been observed (i.e. E[V | buy, buy, and a third buy]).

outputs.name: ask_initial
outputs.description: E[V | first trade is a buy]

outputs.name: bid_initial
outputs.description: E[V | first trade is a sell]

solution: P(buy|H) = 0.3+0.35 = 0.65, P(buy|L) = 0.35. P(H|buy) = 0.650 so ask = 100.60; symmetrically bid = 99.40; spread = 1.20. After two buys P(H) = 0.7752; conditioning on a third buy gives P(H) = 0.8650 and ask = 101.460. Quotes drift toward 102 as order flow reveals information.

checks.name: dealer expected profit on a buy at the initial ask is zero
a buy followed by a sell returns the posterior to the prior (symmetric design)

wrong_answers.label: keep the ask fixed after observing buys
wrong_answers.reason: Each buy raises the probability that the value is high; a Bayesian dealer must raise the ask.

wrong_answers.label: quote the posterior mean after two buys without conditioning on the next buy
wrong_answers.reason: The ask must break even conditional on the next trade being a buy, which is itself informative.

limitations: Single-unit trades, no inventory cost, fixed informed share.

title: Deflated Sharpe ratio for the best of 25 backtests
mechanism: Probabilistic Sharpe ratio with skew/kurtosis correction evaluated against a selection-adjusted benchmark
decision_relevance: Whether the chosen backtest survives after accounting for how many were tried
prompt: A researcher selects the best of N=25 independent backtest variants. The selected variant has a monthly (non-annualised) Sharpe ratio of 0.35 over T=72 months, with return skewness -0.6 and kurtosis 5.0 (raw, not excess). The variance of the monthly Sharpe estimates across the 25 variants is 0.01. Use the probabilistic Sharpe ratio PSR(SR*) = Phi[(SR - SR*) sqrt(T-1) / sqrt(1 - g3 SR + (g4-1)/4 SR^2)] and the selection benchmark SR* = sqrt(V) [(1-g) Z(1-1/N) + g Z(1-1/(N e))] with g=0.5772 the Euler-Mascheroni constant. Report (1) SR*, (2) the deflated Sharpe ratio probability PSR(SR*), (3) the undeflated PSR(0), and (4) whether the null of no skill is rejected at 95% (DSR >= 0.95).

outputs.name: sr0_benchmark
outputs.description: expected max Sharpe under the null

solution: Z(0.96) = 1.7507, Z(1-1/(25e)) = 2.1777; SR* = 0.1 x [...] = 0.1997. Denominator sqrt(1 + 0.6 x 0.35 + 1 x 0.35^2) = 1.1543. DSR = Phi((0.35-0.1997) x sqrt(71) / denom) = 0.8637 (< 0.95, not rejected), whereas the undeflated PSR(0) = 0.9947 would have looked convincing.

checks.name: Gaussian limit (skew 0, kurt 3) of PSR(0) equals the Lo iid Sharpe t-test probability
deflation lowers the probability

wrong_answers.label: no deflation for selection
wrong_answers.reason: The best of 25 trials would show a Sharpe near SR* even with zero skill everywhere.

wrong_answers.label: plug the annualised Sharpe into the monthly formula
wrong_answers.reason: T counts monthly observations, so the Sharpe must be at the same monthly frequency.

limitations: Benchmark formula assumes independent trials; the PSR uses a normal approximation.

title: FDR versus FWER control over twelve signal tests
mechanism: Benjamini-Hochberg step-up rule contrasted with Bonferroni and Holm step-down thresholds
decision_relevance: How many candidate signals to carry forward under different error-control philosophies
prompt: Twelve candidate trading signals were each tested against a null of zero mean return, giving the two-sided p-values listed. Report (1) the number of signals declared discoveries by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure at false discovery rate q=0.10 (largest k such that the k-th smallest p-value is at most k q/m, all smaller p-values are then rejected), (2) the p-value cutoff, i.e. the k-th smallest p-value at that k, (3) the number rejected by Bonferroni at family-wise level 0.05, and (4) the number rejected by Holm step-down at 0.05.
solution: BH thresholds k x 0.1/12: the 8th smallest p = 0.06 <= 0.0667 while the 9th (0.11) fails, so k = 8 and cutoff 0.06. Note the 5th smallest (0.045 > 0.0417) fails locally yet is still rejected because BH steps up from the largest passing k. Bonferroni 0.05/12 = 0.00417 rejects 2; Holm rejects 3 (0.0048 <= 0.05/10 but 0.013 > 0.05/9).

checks.name: counting p-values at or below the BH cutoff reproduces the number of discoveries
Holm rejects at least as many as Bonferroni and BH at least as many as Holm

wrong_answers.label: stop BH at the first failing p-value (step-down misreading)
wrong_answers.reason: BH is a step-up rule: a locally failing p-value is still rejected if a larger k passes.

wrong_answers.label: apply a single threshold q/m to all tests
wrong_answers.reason: That is Bonferroni at level q, which controls the family-wise rate and is far more conservative than FDR.

limitations: BH assumes independent or positively dependent tests.

title: Kalman local-level filter for a drifting signal mean
family: time-series state estimation and mean reversion
mechanism: Scalar Kalman recursion for a random-walk state with closed-form steady-state gain via the Riccati equation
decision_relevance: How much weight to give the newest observation of a time-varying alpha
prompt: The true expected monthly return mu_t of a signal follows a random walk mu_t = mu_{t-1} + w_t with Var(w)=0.0004. Each month a noisy realisation y_t = mu_t + v_t is observed with Var(v)=0.01. Both innovation sequences are zero-mean Gaussian, independent across time and of each other and of mu_0. The initial prior is mu_0 ~ N(0, 0.01). Six observations are given (decimal monthly returns). Run the Kalman filter (predict then update each month). Report (1) the filtered mean after the sixth observation, (2) the filtered variance after the sixth observation, (3) the steady-state Kalman gain, and (4) the half-life in months of the equivalent exponentially weighted average implied by the steady-state gain (ln 0.5 / ln(1-K)).

outputs.name: filtered_mean
outputs.description: posterior mean of mu after 6 updates

solution: Each step: P_pred = P + 0.0004, K = P_pred/(P_pred + 0.01), m += K(y - m), P = (1-K)P_pred. After six updates m = 0.07621, P = 0.002072. Steady state solves P_pred^2 - q P_pred - q r = 0 giving P_pred = 0.002210 and K = 0.1810; the filter behaves like an EWMA with half-life 3.47 months. Treating the mean as fixed would instead give 0.07429 with a gain shrinking toward zero.

checks.name: Riccati closed form vs 500-step iteration of the predicted variance
filtered variance after six steps is still above the steady-state filtered variance and below the prior

wrong_answers.label: assume a constant mean (state noise zero)
wrong_answers.reason: With no state noise the filter converges to the sample mean and stops adapting to drift.

wrong_answers.label: gain = q/(q+r)
wrong_answers.reason: The steady-state gain depends on the predicted variance from the Riccati equation, not the raw noise ratio.

limitations: Scalar model with known noise variances; in practice they are estimated by maximum likelihood.

title: Entry threshold for an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck spread trade
family: time-series state estimation and mean reversion
mechanism: Mean first-passage times of an OU process to trade off profit per cycle against cycle length
decision_relevance: Choosing an entry band for a mean-reversion strategy with round-trip costs
prompt: A spread follows dX = -theta X dt + sigma dW with theta=0.05 per trading day and sigma=1.0 spread points per sqrt(day), long-run mean 0. A strategy waits at a flat position until |X| first reaches a threshold a (starting from X=0), enters one unit against the deviation, and exits when X first returns to 0, then waits again. Each round trip earns a spread points minus a cost of 0.4 points. Use the exact mean first-passage times of the OU process: E[time from 0 to |X|=a] = (sqrt(pi)/theta) * integral_0^{u} exp(x^2) erf(x) dx and E[time from a to 0] = (sqrt(pi)/theta) * integral_0^{u} exp(x^2) erfc(x) dx with u = a sqrt(theta)/sigma. The universe of thresholds is the finite grid {1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 5}. Report (1) the grid threshold maximising expected profit per day (profit per cycle divided by expected cycle time), (2) that maximal profit rate in points per day, (3) the expected cycle time in days at that threshold, and (4) the stationary standard deviation of the spread.

outputs.name: best_threshold
outputs.description: grid threshold with the highest profit rate

outputs.name: cycle_days_at_best
outputs.description: expected wait plus expected reversion time

solution: Profit rate (a-0.4)/[T_out(a)+T_rev(a)] over the grid: a=1.0: 0.0744; a=1.5: 0.0891; a=2.0: 0.0942; a=2.5: 0.0951; a=3.0: 0.0932; a=3.5: 0.0895; a=4.0: 0.0844; a=5.0: 0.0711. Best a = 2.5 with 0.0951 points/day and cycle 22.09 days; stationary sd = 3.162. Without cost the optimum would be a = 1.0, so costs push the entry band wider.

checks.name: small-threshold limit of T(a->0) equals sqrt(pi) a/(sigma sqrt(theta))
stationary variance equals the long-horizon OU variance sigma^2(1-e^{-2 theta t})/(2 theta)
cycle time increases monotonically on the grid

wrong_answers.label: maximise profit per trade (largest threshold)
wrong_answers.reason: Wider bands earn more per trade but trade so rarely that profit per unit time falls.

wrong_answers.label: choose the threshold ignoring costs, then report its actual net performance
wrong_answers.reason: Without costs the optimal band is narrower; the 0.4-point cost reduces the net profit rate at the narrow band enough to change the optimum.

limitations: Grid optimum only; one unit position, no slippage on entry, exact OU parameters.

title: Execution urgency after time-varying liquidity and price risk
mechanism: finite Almgren-style schedule with post-trade inventory risk and a binding participation cap
decision_relevance: Balance expected implementation cost against risk while liquidating a position on a feasible schedule.
prompt: All inputs are explicitly synthetic. Calculator or code use is permitted. Liquidate all opening inventory in four slices at times0,1,2,3. Each slice sells an integer number of lots between zero and its stated maximum; these finite schedules are the complete permitted universe. No purchases or residual final inventory. Expected temporary cost in slice i is temporary_cost_i*n_i^2 USD and linear cost is linear_cost*n_i; total permanent cost is permanent_coefficient*initial_inventory_lots^2/2 USD, independent of schedule.
